Verdict

VerdictNO-GORisk tier 3 of 3

Don't launch yet: four things block it. The most serious is that the opening time can silently be wrong, so the sale could open hours early or stay shut at midnight. And the shop has never taken a real card payment: the connections to the real payment provider, sign-in and database aren't built yet. The previous review found 23 problems; 16 are now fixed and verified, and 7 are still open in some form (partly fixed, accepted as a risk, or waiting on a condition). Together with the new problems this review found, the open ones are listed under What to fix.

If you launched anyway

The sale might open before the email goes out, letting bots and early visitors take the pairs, or stay shut while 3,000 people wait. Nobody knows whether a real card payment goes through, so the first real customer is the first test. Customers get no confirmation email. If something breaks during the sale, the documented way back (rollback) fails, and nobody is named to be woken up.

What has to happen

#What has to happenWhoHow bigWhen
1 Blocker Make the opening time impossible to set wrong: one place where it's set, only full times with a time zone, and the time in force shown in the admin answer and in the log. details: ARC-11 A-09 DeveloperSmall: a few hoursBefore launch
2 Blocker Connect the real database, sign-in and card payment, have a reviewer check them, then make one small real purchase and refund. details: INT-01 S-06 D-13 Developer, with the providers you choose; you make the test purchaseOne to two weeks, depending on the providersBefore launch
3 Blocker Show that backups can be restored, that an alert reaches a named person, and who is on call on launch night.
Required for a high-risk launch (risk tier 3). details: OPS-04 O-03 O-05 O-10		 Hosting provider or developer; you name the on-call personAbout a day, once recovery targets are agreedBefore launch
4 Blocker Build the operator tools the launch-night runbook relies on, try each once, and make the way back to the previous version work.
Required for a high-risk launch: without them, problems on the night can't be handled. details: OPS-08 OPS-09		 DeveloperMedium: one to two daysBefore launch
5 Condition Set up a test copy of the shop (staging) with its own database, keys and test payments, so the runbook and the real payment can be rehearsed safely. details: R-06 Hosting provider or developerAbout a dayBefore launch
6 Condition Run one copy of the app only, and set the load balancer's idle timeout below 65 seconds. details: A-06 O-09 Hosting provider or developerSmallAt launch

8 Condition Repeat the load test on production-sized machines, with the load generator on its own machine. details: P-02 DeveloperHalf a dayBefore launch

Decisions only you can make

  • Choose the payment provider, sign-in provider and email provider (or decide to launch without confirmation emails). details: INT-01 ARC-07
  • Agree how much order data you could afford to lose, and how fast the shop must be back after a failure (for example: at most 5 minutes of orders, back within 30 minutes). details: R-07 OPS-04
  • Set the sale date. If the sale page goes live more than 25 days before it, the page reloads itself non-stop until PERF-04 is fixed. details: PERF-04
  • Decide how long a payment may stay "confirming" before the pair goes back on sale and the shopper is told. details: ARC-10
  • Accept, in writing and until a date, running only one copy of the app on launch night. details: ARC-06
  • Decide whether to remove the page's mentions of an order history and an email, or have them built. details: ARC-14
  • Sign this page once the blockers are done.

When you could launch An estimate, not a promise: about two to three weeks of developer work once the providers are chosen, most of it connecting real payments, plus the time to book a security test. Set the sale date after that.

What customers would notice today

  • No confirmation email after buying: emails are queued but never sent (ARC-07).
  • The sign-in box stays on the page after signing in, and the stock count doesn't change after buying (ARC-15).
  • The page mentions an order history and an email that don't exist (ARC-14).
  • If the page goes live more than about 25 days before the sale, it reloads itself non-stop (PERF-04).
  • Shoppers who sign in early and open a new tab are signed out (OPS-03).

How to read this page

Product owner
You: the person this review is for, who decides whether to launch and signs.
Blocker
Launch can't happen until it's done.
Condition
Also required, at the time shown, but not a reason to stop launch on its own.
Cannot verify
The reviewer didn't have what was needed to check it. It is not a pass: each one says what's needed.
Risk tier 3
High risk: the app takes payments itself, holds sensitive data, or launches with a big rush. Every Critical or High problem blocks launch, and backups, alerts and an on-call person must be shown.
Codes
Codes like ARC-11 or OPS-08 are problems found (see What to fix). Codes like A-09 or O-03 are checklist items (under "Full checklist" in each section).
Evidence A, B, C
A: the reviewer ran or measured it. B: the reviewer inspected the code or settings. C: someone's statement, which never counts as proof.
Dotted underline
Hover over it, or tap it, for an explanation.

What to fix

24 open problems, blockers first, then by severity. 16 more already fixed and verified are listed at the end.

  • INT-01HighBlocks launchOpen · Confirmed

    The real database, sign-in and card payment aren't connected

    Impact
    The code talks only to stand-ins: a local SQLite file instead of the hosted Postgres database, a test sign-in that accepts any email, and a payment simulator. Card details, 3-D Secure, declines and refunds have never been handled, so the first real customer would be the first test.
    Who
    Developer, with the providers the product owner chooses
    Where
    Database: shared/db.mjs (SQLite stand-in). Sign-in: POST /api/login test stub. Payment: fixed/server.mjs:299-310 (calls the simulator).
    Fix
    Connect hosted Postgres, the chosen sign-in provider and the chosen payment provider (including the provider's lookup call and refunds); have a reviewer check them; then make a purchase, a decline and a refund in the provider's test mode, and one small real purchase and refund.
    Done when
    The race test and acceptance tests pass against staging with the real database and the provider's test mode, and the provider's records match the shop's orders for one real purchase and refund.
  • ARC-11HighBlocks launchOpen · Confirmed

    The opening time can silently be wrong

    Impact
    If the opening time is changed after the first start, the server keeps the old one while its log shows the new one, so the sale can open hours early or stay shut at midnight. A date without a time zone, or text like "Nov 27" (read as 2001), opens the sale at once.
    Who
    Developer
    Where
    fixed/server.mjs:111-114, :646, :24-25, :537-539
    Fix
    One source of truth, only full times with a time zone, and show the time in force in the log and the admin answer. Effort: small.
    Done when
    A test starts the app twice on the same database with a changed opening time and sees the new time in force; "Nov 27", "1" and a date without a time zone are refused; both run in CI.
  • OPS-04MediumBlocks launchPartly fixed · Likely

    The launch-night safety nets haven't been shown

    Impact
    Backups, error tracking, alerts and on-call are listed in the runbook but not evidenced.
    Who
    Hosting provider or developer; product owner names the on-call person and agrees recovery targets
    Where
    fixed/RUNBOOK.md:9-10
    Fix
    Show a tested restore, a received test alert and the rota.
    Done when
    A restore log, a received test alert, and the on-call rota are attached to the review.
  • OPS-08MediumBlocks launchOpen · Confirmed

    The runbook relies on tools that don't exist

    Impact
    Loading stock, resolving a stuck payment, exporting addresses and comparing charges with orders have no tool.
    Who
    Developer
    Where
    fixed/RUNBOOK.md steps for loading stock, resolving a stuck payment, exporting addresses and comparing charges with orders
    Fix
    Build each tool and try it once.
    Done when
    Each runbook step names a command that exists, and a rehearsal log shows each one run once.
    Depends on
    INT-01 (comparing charges with orders needs the real provider) · a staging copy to rehearse on
  • OPS-09MediumBlocks launchOpen · Confirmed

    Rolling back to the previous release fails

    Impact
    The rollback the runbook prescribes fails at start-up, so the shop stays down when things are already bad.
    Who
    Developer
    Where
    fixed/RUNBOOK.md:27 (rollback step); start-up migrations in fixed/server.mjs:73-115
    Fix
    Make the previous release start against the new schema, or roll forward with a tested fix.
    Done when
    The previous release starts against the current database in a test, or the runbook replaces rollback with a tried roll-forward step.
  • ARC-10MediumAgree a date before launchOpen · Confirmed

    A payment that never resolves stays "confirming" forever

    Impact
    A payment error that retrying can't fix keeps the pair reserved indefinitely: the whole stock could be locked with nothing sold. A warning is written to the log after 10 minutes, but nothing yet delivers log warnings to a person.
    Who
    Developer
    Where
    fixed/server.mjs:294-387 (charge, settle, reconciler)
    Fix
    Look the payment up instead of re-sending it, give "confirming" a deadline, then release the pair and tell the shopper.
    Done when
    A test where the provider keeps failing ends with the pair released and the shopper told, within the agreed deadline.
    Depends on
    INT-01 · the product owner's deadline for "confirming"
  • SEC-03MediumAgree a date before launchPartly fixed · Confirmed

    One person can still buy several pairs, and nothing slows bots

    Impact
    A second mailbox or a re-spelt address buys another pair.
    Who
    Developer
    Where
    fixed/server.mjs:411-415 (one per customer and per address)
    Fix
    Firmer identity for the limit, and a waiting room or bot protection in front of the drop.
    Done when
    A second mailbox or a re-spelt address can't buy a second pair in a test; a bot-protection or waiting-room service is in front of the drop.
  • SEC-04MediumCondition: Before launchCondition · Confirmed

    Production safety depends on one setting nobody sets

    Impact
    Started without NODE_ENV=production, the shop runs with demo secrets, test sign-in and the reset route switched on.
    Who
    Developer
    Where
    fixed/server.mjs:10-52
    Fix
    Make production the default: refuse to start with demo values unless demo mode is switched on explicitly, so forgetting one setting can't open the shop with demo settings. Add a real production start command.
    Done when
    Starting without NODE_ENV and without an explicit demo switch fails.
  • SEC-06MediumAgree a date before launchOpen · Confirmed

  • PERF-03MediumAgree a date before launchOpen · Confirmed

    One signed-in script can tie up the database

    Impact
    Unlimited signed-in reads can starve checkout during the rush.
    Who
    Developer
    Where
    fixed/server.mjs:503-518

  • PERF-04MediumAgree a date before launchOpen · Confirmed

    The page reloads non-stop if the sale is more than ~25 days away

    Impact
    Browser timers overflow above about 25 days, so every open page reloads the product non-stop and hammers the server. The sale date isn't set yet: if the page goes live more than 25 days before the sale, this happens from day one.
    Who
    Developer
    Where
    shared/public/app.js:46-47
    Fix
    Cap the countdown timer and re-check periodically.
    Done when
    A page loaded 60 days before opening re-checks no more than once a minute.
  • OPS-03MediumAgree a date before launchPartly fixed · Confirmed

    Impact

    Who

    Where
    shared/public/app.js (session in sessionStorage)

Product

A one-page flash sale for 100 pairs of limited-edition sneakers at $49.99, one pair per customer. Shoppers sign in, enter a shipping address and press Buy; the sale opens at midnight after an email blast. (This is the worked example in this repository: the demo app's fixed/ version, after two rounds of review and fixes.)

Users Public shoppers (about 3,000 in the first 60 seconds), the small team running the sale, and admins with a shared token.

Out of scope

  • The production identity provider and card-payment integration: they are not in the repository.
  • Cloud and load-balancer configuration.
  • The simulated database and payment provider themselves.

Risk tier 3 The app calls the card provider's charge API itself, so amounts, repeat-safety, time-outs and reconciliation are its own job, and the whole sale happens in a promoted 60-second rush. High risk: the app takes payments itself, holds sensitive data, or launches with a big rush. Every Critical or High problem blocks launch, and backups, alerts and an on-call person must be shown.

AI coding agents or assistants write or change the codeusers sign instores personal data (names, emails, addresses, messages, health, financial)takes payments, issues refunds or credits, or holds balancessells or allocates something limited (stock, seats, coupons, slots)has admin or staff functionsexpects a launch, promotion or other traffic spike

Demo: the main journeys

J1 Buy one pair

A signed-in shopper, sale open, pairs in stock

  1. Open the sale page.
  2. Sign in with an email address (a test sign-in in the demo; a magic link in production).
  3. Enter a shipping address.
  4. Press Buy now.

Expected "Order #… confirmed — $49.99 charged." One order, one charge, at the listed price.

Proved by acceptance criteria AC-02 AC-03 AC-11

J2 Arrive before the sale opens

A signed-in shopper before midnight

  1. Open the sale page before the opening time.
  2. Sign in and enter an address.

Expected The page says when the sale opens and the button reads "Not open yet". A purchase sent directly to the server is refused.

Proved by acceptance criteria AC-12

J3 Double-click Buy

A signed-in shopper who clicks twice

  1. Sign in and enter an address.
  2. Double-click Buy now.

Expected Exactly one order and one charge. The second click is told the shopper already has an order.

Proved by acceptance criteria AC-04 AC-07

J4 Pay while the payment provider is slow

A signed-in shopper while the provider isn't answering

  1. Press Buy now while the payment provider is slow or down.
  2. Wait; don't pay again.

Expected Within 5 seconds: "confirming your payment, please don't pay again". When the provider recovers: exactly one paid order and one charge.

Proved by acceptance criteria AC-08

J5 Sold out

Any visitor after the last pair is sold

  1. Open the sale page when stock is 0.

Expected "Sold out" is shown and the button can't be pressed.

Proved by acceptance criteria AC-05

How to run it

Can a reviewer start work from the README alone?

For whoever runs the app: usually the developer.

Prerequisites

  • Node.js 22.13 or later (the app uses only built-in modules, including node:sqlite)
  • For the tests: npm, and Playwright 1.56 (installed by the suite); k6 1.3 for load and race tests

Commands

Set up
git clone https://github.com/johnsonnoronathan/everyone_is_a_product_manager
cd everyone_is_a_product_manager
Start
node demo/flash-sale/run.mjs fixed
Open
http://127.0.0.1:3000
Test
cd demo/flash-sale/acceptance && npm ci && npx playwright install chromium
VARIANT=fixed npx playwright test --repeat-each=3
# race and load tests: see .claude/skills/peak-traffic-test (needs k6)
Reset test data
curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:3000/api/admin/reset -H 'x-admin-token: demo-admin-token' -H 'content-type: application/json' -d '{"stock":100}'

Test copy (staging) None provided.

Test accounts

RoleHow to sign in
ShopperType any email address into the sign-in box. This test sign-in exists only with DEMO_LOGIN=1 and is refused in production.
AdminSend the header x-admin-token: demo-admin-token (the demo value run.mjs sets).

7

Architecture

Is the structure sound for the agreed requirements?

One Node.js program behind a load balancer, with no framework and no third-party packages. It keeps orders in a database, calls the payment provider directly with one repeat-safe key per order, and runs two background jobs (settling payments whose outcome is unknown, and sending confirmation emails from a queue) plus small housekeeping timers. In this demo a local SQLite file stands in for the hosted Postgres database a real deployment would use, and a simulator stands in for the payment provider.

A deliberately small design: one process, no packages, every decision on the server. It handles slow payments correctly now. The weak points are the opening time, which can be silently wrong, and a rollback that fails.

flowchart LR
  Shopper["Shopper's browser"] -->|HTTPS| LB["Load balancer"]
  Admin["Staff: shared admin token"] -->|HTTPS| LB
  LB --> App["Node.js app (one instance)"]
  App -->|"pool of 10, 1 s wait"| DB[("Postgres: orders, stock, settings, email queue")]
  App -->|"3 s limit, key per order"| Pay["Payment provider"]
  Recon["Reconciler, every 5 s"] --> DB
  Recon -->|"same key"| Pay
  Mailer["Email sender, every 1 s"] --> DB
  Mailer -.->|"not built yet"| Mail["Email provider"]
  IdP["Sign-in provider (not in repo)"] -.-> Shopper

ReconcilerSettles orders whose payment outcome is unknown, using the same repeat-safe keyTimer in the app process

Decisions

DecisionWhyAlternativesDownsides
One process, no framework, no packagesSmall surface, nothing to patchExpress or Next.js; a hosted checkoutRate limits and caches live in one process: run one instance
A payment time-out is "unknown", not "failed"The provider may have charged after the app gave up (57 charges for 39 pairs in round 1)Release the pair on time-out (round 1)Needs a reconciler, and a deadline for outcomes that never resolve (ARC-10)
Emails through a database outboxA slow email provider never slows checkout, and no email is lost on restartSend inside the request (naive version)Needs a sender with retries per email

Business rules

Can the data become wrong?

Stock, duplicates and the price are enforced by the database and proven by a 1,000-buyer race. The gaps are input that's accepted when it should be refused (the opening time) and payments that can stay "confirming" forever.

IDRuleEnforced byProved by
BR-1Never sell more pairs than are in stockAtomic stock = stock - 1 WHERE stock > 0 in the same transaction as the order, plus CHECK (stock >= 0)Race test: 1,000 buyers × 2 clicks → 100 sold (AC-07)
BR-2One pair per customerUnique index on product and customer among live ordersAC-04; race test: 100 distinct customers
BR-3One pair per shipping addressUnique index on a simplified addressNo test. The review found different non-Latin addresses collide (ARC-12)
BR-4Customers pay the listed pricePrice read from the database; the browser's price is ignoredAC-03: a request saying $0.01 was charged $49.99
BR-5Every paid order has exactly one chargeOne repeat-safe payment key per order; a time-out is "unknown" and settled with the same keySlow provider: 40 charges for 40 orders, 60 for 60 (AC-08)
BR-6Every order has a shipping addressServer requires 10–300 charactersAC-11
BR-7Nobody buys before the opening time or while the sale is pausedServer checks the sale settings on every buyAC-12, AC-13. But the opening time itself can be silently wrong (ARC-11)

Harness: tests, automatic checks and AI-agent instructions

Will the next change, by a person or an AI agent, keep the project correct?

The tests that exist check orders, charges and messages, cover payment failures and double clicks, and pass reliably in CI; they don't check what should disappear from the page. Performance

Will it hold the expected traffic and stay correct?

The expected rush passes in every run with a lot of room to spare, the race never oversold, and a slow payment provider no longer causes double charges. Capacity above 150% isn't proven, because everything ran on one laptop-class machine.

Target 600 requests/s (3,000 visitors in 60 s, 3× peaks); product page p95 ≤ 500 ms, buy p95 ≤ 1.5 s

Tested on One 4-core machine running the app, the payment simulator and the load generator together

Slow partner

With the payment provider answering in about 3 seconds: 40 charges for 40 paid orders, and 60 for 60 in a second run; repeat clicks were refused. The previous version charged 57 times for 39 pairs.

The expected peak passes in every run, with p95 at or under 5 ms. 150% passed in two of three runs, so headroom of 1.5× and above isn't reliably proven on this machine: repeat the test on production-sized machines, with the load generator on its own machine.

Quality history: problems that keep coming back

What has gone wrong before, and is it fixed for good?

The same kinds of problem came back across three reviews, and several problems were introduced by fixes. None is yet caught fully automatically: the counts are in the tiles below.

Period Three reviews, 2026-10-16 to 2026-10-17, and the git history of demo/flash-sale/ (10 commits, 2026-10-16 to 2026-10-18).

Sources

  • Three review reports on this app: the first version (30 problems), round 1 (23) and round 2 (all 23 re-checked, plus 13 new): demo/flash-sale/sample-reports/. Problems are labelled Review 1, 2 and 3 below. Problem codes restart in each review: "Review 1 PERF-03" is not the same problem as PERF-03 under What to fix.
  • Git history of demo/flash-sale/, scanned with history-scan.mjs: 10 commits, all with an AI co-author. Five look like fixes, but the two that matter bundle a whole round each (79 and 29 files), so git can't separate individual defects here and the review reports are the defect record.
  • No issue tracker or incident log exists for the demo.

Problems that came back (6 kinds)

Outside calls whose outcome is unknown

Partly caught automatically

Seen 4 times

  • Review 1 PERF-03 No time limit on the payment call: one slow charge holds the request for 30 s.
  • Review 2 ARC-01 A time-out was treated as a failure: 57 charges for 39 pairs. Introduced by the fix for the missing time limit. Introduced by a fix
  • Review 2 ARC-02 Database busy right after payment: the shopper is told "very busy" and the paid order is stuck.
  • Review 3 ARC-10 An error that retrying can't fix leaves orders "confirming" forever.

Why it keeps happening Every outside call was modelled as success or failure. "Unknown" (timed out, but the provider may still have charged) wasn't a state, so each fix moved the problem: no time limit, then a time-out treated as failure, then "unknown" with no deadline. The tests' payment stub never completed a charge after the app gave up, so the tests couldn't see it.

What catches the next one A realistic payment simulator (finishes abandoned charges, hangs 2% of calls), used by acceptance test AC-08 in CI and by the slow-provider runs.

Checked AC-08 fails on the round-1 code and passes on round 2; slow provider: 40 charges for 40 orders.

Rule for AI agents Every outside call: a time limit, a repeat-safe key, and an explicit "unknown" state settled by the reconciler with the same key, with a deadline.

Bad input crashes the app or is quietly accepted

Partly caught automatically

Seen 6 times

  • Review 1 SEC-07 Malformed JSON crashes the whole site.
  • Review 1 A malformed Host header crashes the server.
  • Review 2 SEC-01 One GET // crashes the shop. Introduced by the fix for the Host header. Introduced by a fix
  • Review 2 SEC-05 A request body of null gives a 500 error.
  • Review 3 ARC-11 "Nov 27" is accepted as 27 November 2001 and opens the sale.
  • Review 3 ARC-12 The address check drops every non-Latin letter, so different addresses collide.

Why it keeps happening Each handler parses its own input with forgiving built-ins (new URL, JSON.parse, new Date, a regular expression), and each fix patched the one input that failed. There is no single validation layer and no test that sends malformed input.

What catches the next one Code-scanning rules url-parse-outside-try and json-parse-in-stream-callback; the reviewer's malformed-path script (7 paths, all answered 400).

Checked The rules' own tests run in CI, but the rules aren't run against the app in CI, and the malformed-input script isn't in the test suite.

Rule for AI agents Parse every input once, strictly, at the edge; refuse rather than guess; add each new input to the malformed-input test.

Settings and data that must survive restarts and deploys

Not caught automatically

Seen 7 times

  • Review 1 ARC-02 Every start-up recreates the database and deletes all orders.
  • Review 1 ARC-04 Settings and secrets live in the code.
  • Review 2 ARC-05 Every start still deletes all orders and resets stock.
  • Review 2 SEC-02 A one-call "delete every order" endpoint ships to production.
  • Review 2 SEC-04 Test sign-in and demo secrets can reach production.
  • Review 3 ARC-11 Changing SALE_STARTS_AT after the first start does nothing, while the log says it did. Introduced by the round-2 fix. Introduced by a fix
  • Review 3 OPS-09 Rolling back to the previous release fails against the new database. Introduced by the round-2 migrations. Introduced by a fix

Why it keeps happening Start-up, settings and deploy behaviour was never specified or tested. Every test starts a fresh app on an empty in-memory database, so the second start, start-up with old data, and the previous release were invisible.

What catches the next one Versioned migrations; production refuses demo switches and placeholder secrets; the reviewer's restart script with a saved database.

Checked A restart keeps orders (verified in round 2), but no restart or rollback test runs in CI, and ARC-11 and OPS-09 are still open.

Rule for AI agents Any change to start-up, settings or the database needs a test that starts the app twice on the same data, and one that starts the previous release.

Business rules checked in code instead of enforced by the database

Partly caught automatically

Seen 6 times

  • Review 1 PERF-01 Stock is read, then written back: 1,962 pairs sold out of 100.
  • Review 1 PERF-02 No one-per-customer limit and no repeat-safety: 963 shoppers charged twice.
  • Review 1 ARC-03 No database constraints for any business rule.
  • Review 1 SEC-05 The price is taken from the browser.
  • Review 2 SEC-03 "One per customer" is really one per email address.
  • Review 3 SEC-03 Still easy to get round, and nothing slows bots down.

Why it keeps happening Rules were written as checks inside request handlers, which simultaneous requests and small variations slip past. Once moved into atomic updates and unique indexes they held; the identity behind "one per customer" is still weak.

What catches the next one Atomic stock update, unique indexes and CHECK (stock >= 0), with the race test in CI.

Checked Race test in CI on every change: 1,000 buyers, 100 sold, 0 charged twice.

Rule for AI agents Enforce limits with constraints or atomic updates, never check-then-write; the race test must pass.

Screen behaviour no test looked at closely

Not caught automatically

Seen 5 times

  • Review 2 ARC-08 The page gets stuck when the server is busy or the session has expired.
  • Review 2 ARC-09 Pairs returned after a failed payment are never offered again (found by a test).
  • Review 3 ARC-15 The sign-in box never disappears; it has been there since the first version.
  • Review 3 PERF-04 A countdown longer than about 25 days reloads the page non-stop. Introduced by the round-2 countdown. Introduced by a fix
  • Review 3 ARC-14 The page points to an order history and an email that don't exist.

Why it keeps happening The acceptance tests check what should appear, never what should disappear or change, and nothing tests the page's timers and error paths. The page was reviewed through the server's eyes.

What catches the next one Guidance "assert what should disappear, too" added to the acceptance-test skill.

Checked Not applied to this suite yet: no test checks that the sign-in box hides.

Rule for AI agents For every change of state on the page, test what appears and what disappears.

Operations promised on paper but not in tools

Not caught automatically

Seen 5 times

  • Review 1 OPS-01 No error tracking, uptime monitoring or alerts.
  • Review 1 OPS-02 No backups or recovery.
  • Review 2 OPS-04 The launch-night safety nets aren't in evidence.
  • Review 3 OPS-04 Still listed in the runbook, still not shown.
  • Review 3 OPS-08 The runbook relies on tools that don't exist: loading stock, resolving a stuck payment, exporting addresses, comparing charges with orders.

Why it keeps happening Operations were written down as intentions (a runbook, a checklist) but never rehearsed, so missing tools and broken steps stayed invisible until a reviewer tried them.

What catches the next one Checklist rule: every runbook step must be backed by a tool that exists and has been tried.

Checked No rehearsal has been run yet.

Rule for AI agents Don't add a runbook step without the command that performs it and a log of it being tried.

Not checked

  • Production sign-in and card payments. Not in the repository. Card collection, 3-D Secure, declines, refunds and the provider's lookup API were not checked. This blocks launch until reviewed and a real purchase and refund are made.
  • Production database and infrastructure: Postgres, backups, the load balancer (HTTPS, idle timeout), CDN and firewall.
  • The real database. A local SQLite file stood in for hosted Postgres, so the database rules (stock, one per customer) were proven on SQLite only, and a real deployment needs a Postgres connection that isn't in the code.
  • Real capacity. Everything ran on one machine against simulators; two app instances were not run.
  • Email sending: not built.
  • Privacy and compliance: privacy notice, consent, data deletion (GDPR, CCPA) and card-industry (PCI DSS) scope.
  • Accessibility beyond the automated check on the sale page.
  • Method. An AI-assisted review lowers risk; it doesn't prove there are no vulnerabilities. At tier 3 an independent penetration test is recommended.
16

Glossary

Evidence grade
A: the reviewer ran or measured it. B: the reviewer read the code or configuration itself. C: someone's statement only, which never counts as proof.
Risk tier
1 low, 2 standard, 3 high. It decides which criteria are mandatory and which problems block launch.
p95
95% of requests were faster than this.
Race test
Many simulated buyers press Buy at the same moment, to check that limited stock is never oversold.
Repeat-safe key (idempotency key)
A label sent with a payment so the provider charges once, even if the request is sent again.
Reconciler
A background job that settles payments whose outcome is unknown.
Outbox
A table of emails waiting to be sent, so none are lost on a restart.
Migration
A numbered change to the database structure.
Rollback
Going back to the previous release.
Load balancer
The front door that passes requests to the app.
Agent instruction file
AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md or similar: what AI coding agents read before changing the code.
Hotspot
A file that needed many fixes; bugs cluster there.
Root cause
Why a kind of problem keeps happening, as opposed to the last instance of it.
Control
An automatic check (test, rule, constraint) that catches the next instance of a problem.
Blocker
Something that must be done before launch.
Condition
Something else that's required, at the time shown, but not a reason to stop launch on its own.
Runbook
A step-by-step guide for whoever looks after the shop during the sale: what to watch, and what to do when something goes wrong.
Staging
A test copy of the shop with test data, separate from the live one.
Production
The live shop that real customers use.
CI (continuous integration)
Automatic checks and tests that run on every change to the code.
Commit
One saved version of the code. The review applies to exactly one.
Harness
Everything that keeps the next change correct: tests, automatic checks, and the instructions AI coding assistants follow.
Instance
One running copy of the app.
Penetration test
Security specialists try to break into the app, with permission.
Confirmed / Likely
Confirmed: the reviewer reproduced the problem or traced it fully. Likely: strong evidence in the code, not reproduced.
Accepted risk
The owner knowingly accepts a problem until a set date.
Rate limit
A cap on how often one person or program can do something, to stop abuse.
Magic link
Signing in by clicking a link sent by email, instead of a password.
